questions.title: Borrowed perimeter
questions.stem:
A rectangle measures 9 cm by 5 cm. A square has exactly the same perimeter as this rectangle.

What is the area of the square?

![A 9 cm by 5 cm rectangle next to a square whose side length is not given.](asset:q1-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The two shapes share their *perimeter*, not their area. Use the perimeter to find the square’s side first; only then can its area be found.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Perimeter of the rectangle = 9 + 5 + 9 + 5 = 28 cm.
2. The square has the same perimeter, 28 cm, made of four equal sides.
3. One side of the square = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 cm.
4. Area of the square = 7 × 7 = 49 cm².

**Calculation**

- Perimeter = 2 × (9 + 5) = 28 cm
- Side = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 cm
- Area = 7 × 7 = 49 cm²

**Why the method works**

A square’s four sides are equal, so its perimeter fixes its side, and its side fixes its area. Notice that the square’s area (49 cm²) is larger than the rectangle’s (45 cm²) although the perimeters are equal.

**Common trap**

Copying the rectangle’s area (45 cm²), or dividing 28 by 2 instead of 4 — half the perimeter is one length plus one width, not a side of the square.

questions.title: Three in a row
questions.stem:
Three identical squares are placed side by side, each sharing a whole side with its neighbour, to make one rectangle.

The perimeter of this rectangle is 48 cm. Find the area of the rectangle.

![Three identical squares in a row forming one rectangle. No lengths are marked.](asset:q2-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Walk around the outside: you travel along exactly 8 sides of the small squares (3 along the top, 3 along the bottom, 1 at each end). The 2 shared sides lie inside the rectangle and are not part of its perimeter.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Trace the boundary: top 3 sides + right end 1 side + bottom 3 sides + left end 1 side = 8 square-sides.
2. These 8 equal sides make 48 cm, so one side = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm.
3. The rectangle is 3 × 6 = 18 cm long and 6 cm wide.
4. Area = 18 × 6 = 108 cm² (the same as 3 squares of 36 cm²).

**Calculation**

- 8 sides = 48 cm  →  1 side = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 cm
- Rectangle = 18 cm × 6 cm
- Area = 18 × 6 = 108 cm²

**Why the method works**

Perimeter counts only edges that have the outside on one side. A shared side has a square on both sides of it, so it is inside the rectangle.

**Common trap**

Counting all 3 × 4 = 12 sides of the three squares. That gives a side of 4 cm and a wrong area of 48 cm².

questions.title: One cut, two perimeters
questions.stem:
A square with sides of 10 cm is cut along one straight line, parallel to one of its sides, into two rectangles A and B.

Rectangle A has a perimeter of 26 cm. What is the perimeter of rectangle B?

![A 10 cm square cut by one straight line into a narrow rectangle A and a wider rectangle B.](asset:q3-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The cut becomes a side of *both* pieces. So the two perimeters together are more than the square’s perimeter: they include the cut twice.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. The cut runs right across the square, so both pieces are 10 cm tall.
2. Perimeter of A = 10 + 10 + (two widths) = 26 cm, so the two widths of A make 6 cm: A is 3 cm wide.
3. B is 10 − 3 = 7 cm wide and 10 cm tall.
4. Perimeter of B = 2 × (7 + 10) = 34 cm.
5. Second method: A and B together have perimeter 40 (the square) + 2 × 10 (the cut, once for each piece) = 60 cm, so B has 60 − 26 = 34 cm.

**Calculation**

- A: 2 × (10 + w) = 26  →  10 + w = 13  →  w = 3 cm
- B: width = 10 − 3 = 7 cm
- B: 2 × (7 + 10) = 34 cm
- Check: 40 + 2 × 10 − 26 = 34 cm

**Why the method works**

Each piece keeps part of the square’s old boundary and gains the cut as a brand-new side. That is why cutting increases the total length of boundary.

**Common trap**

Thinking the two perimeters add up to the square’s perimeter and answering 40 − 26 = 14 cm. A 10 cm by 4 cm piece would then be needed, which has perimeter 28 cm, not 14 cm.

questions.title: Lines drawn versus boundary
questions.stem:
A rectangle 8 cm long and 6 cm wide is divided into four smaller rectangles by two straight lines. One line joins the midpoints of the two long sides; the other joins the midpoints of the two short sides.

![An 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle divided into four equal smaller rectangles by lines joining midpoints of opposite sides. Equal halves are marked with tick marks.](asset:q4-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: What is the total length of all the lines in the drawing — the outline and the two inside lines?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: What is the sum of the perimeters of the four small rectangles?

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

In (b) every inside line is counted *twice*, because it is a side of the rectangle on each side of it, while the outline is counted only once.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. The outline is the perimeter of the big rectangle: 2 × (8 + 6) = 28 cm.
2. The line joining the midpoints of the two 8 cm sides goes straight across, so it is 6 cm long. The line joining the midpoints of the two 6 cm sides is 8 cm long.
3. (a) Total length drawn = 28 + 6 + 8 = 42 cm.
4. Each small rectangle is half of 8 by half of 6, that is 4 cm by 3 cm, with perimeter 2 × (4 + 3) = 14 cm.
5. (b) Sum of the four perimeters = 4 × 14 = 56 cm.
6. Check: outline once + inside lines twice = 28 + 2 × (6 + 8) = 56 cm.

**Calculation**

- (a) 28 + 6 + 8 = 42 cm
- Small rectangle: 4 cm × 3 cm, perimeter 2 × (4 + 3) = 14 cm
- (b) 4 × 14 = 56 cm
- Check: 28 + 2 × 14 = 56 cm

**Why the method works**

The perimeter of each small rectangle includes the inside lines that border it. Each inside line borders two small rectangles, so the sum of the four perimeters counts it twice; the big outline borders only one small rectangle at each point.

**Common trap**

Answering 28 cm for (b) because “the four pieces make the same big rectangle”, or giving 42 cm for both parts. Total area is unchanged by cutting, but total perimeter is not.

questions.title: Same area, different fence
questions.stem:
A square and a rectangle both have an area of 36 cm². The rectangle’s sides are whole numbers of centimetres, and its perimeter is 30 cm.

![A square and a rectangle, each marked area 36 square centimetres. The drawing is schematic.](asset:q5-fig1)

*Not to scale.*

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How much longer is the rectangle’s perimeter than the square’s perimeter?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: What are the length and width of the rectangle?

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Equal areas do not mean equal perimeters. The rectangle’s sides must satisfy two facts at once: they *multiply* to 36 and *add* to 15 (half of 30).

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Square: side × side = 36, so the side is 6 cm and the perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24 cm.
2. (a) 30 − 24 = 6 cm. (The rectangle’s own sides are not needed for this part.)
3. Rectangle: half of its perimeter is one length plus one width, so length + width = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 cm.
4. Whole-number pairs with product 36: 1 & 36, 2 & 18, 3 & 12, 4 & 9, 6 & 6. Their sums are 37, 20, 15, 13, 12.
5. (b) Only 3 & 12 adds to 15, so the rectangle is 12 cm by 3 cm.

**Calculation**

- Square side = 6 cm (6 × 6 = 36), perimeter = 24 cm
- (a) 30 − 24 = 6 cm
- Length + width = 15, length × width = 36  →  12 and 3
- Check: 2 × (12 + 3) = 30 cm, 12 × 3 = 36 cm²

**Why the method works**

Half the perimeter equals one length plus one width. Listing the factor pairs of the area and testing their sums finds the only rectangle that matches both facts.

**Common trap**

Assuming equal areas give equal perimeters and answering 0 cm for (a). The long, thin 12 × 3 rectangle has a much longer boundary than the square.

questions.title: Squares off the end
questions.stem:
From a rectangle 14 cm long and 9 cm wide, the largest possible square is cut off one end. From the rectangle that is left, the largest possible square is cut off again, as shown.

What is the perimeter of the small rectangle that is left over at the end?

![A 14 cm by 9 cm rectangle divided into a large first square on the left, a smaller second square at the top right, and a left-over piece at the bottom right.](asset:q6-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The largest square that can be cut from a rectangle has a side equal to the rectangle’s *shorter* side. Each cut subtracts the shorter side from the longer one.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. The shorter side of the 14 × 9 rectangle is 9 cm, so the first square is 9 cm by 9 cm.
2. What is left is 14 − 9 = 5 cm wide and still 9 cm long.
3. The shorter side of this 5 × 9 rectangle is 5 cm, so the second square is 5 cm by 5 cm.
4. What is left is 5 cm by 9 − 5 = 4 cm.
5. Perimeter of the left-over rectangle = 2 × (5 + 4) = 18 cm.

**Calculation**

- 14 × 9  →  cut 9 × 9  →  5 × 9 left
- 5 × 9  →  cut 5 × 5  →  5 × 4 left
- Perimeter = 2 × (5 + 4) = 18 cm
- Area check: 81 + 25 + 20 = 126 = 14 × 9

**Why the method works**

A square cut from a rectangle cannot be wider than the rectangle’s shorter side, and a square of exactly that size fits. So each step removes a square whose side is the current shorter side.

**Common trap**

Trying to cut a second 9 cm square from a strip that is only 5 cm wide, or forgetting that the strip left after the first cut is 9 cm long (not 14 cm).

questions.title: Twenty centimetres of string
questions.stem:
A piece of string 20 cm long is laid out as the outline of a rectangle whose sides are whole numbers of centimetres. (A square counts as a rectangle, and a 3 × 7 rectangle is the same as a 7 × 3 rectangle.) Two of the possible rectangles are drawn on a 1 cm grid.

![A 1 centimetre grid showing two rectangles that each have perimeter 20 cm: one 8 cm by 2 cm, one 6 cm by 4 cm.](asset:q7-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How many different rectangles are possible?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: What is the difference between the largest and the smallest possible areas?

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Every rectangle with perimeter 20 cm has length + width = 10 cm. The closer the two sides are to each other, the larger the area.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Half of the perimeter is one length plus one width: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 cm.
2. Whole-number pairs adding to 10: 1 + 9, 2 + 8, 3 + 7, 4 + 6, 5 + 5. (a) That is 5 rectangles.
3. Their areas are 1 × 9 = 9, 2 × 8 = 16, 3 × 7 = 21, 4 × 6 = 24 and 5 × 5 = 25 (all in cm²).
4. Largest area 25 cm² (the square); smallest 9 cm² (the 1 × 9 strip).
5. (b) Difference = 25 − 9 = 16 cm².

**Calculation**

- length + width = 20 ÷ 2 = 10
- areas: 9, 16, 21, 24, 25 (cm²)
- 25 − 9 = 16 cm²

**Why the method works**

Listing all pairs that add to half the perimeter lists every possible rectangle, so nothing is missed. The list shows that one fixed perimeter can surround very different areas.

**Common trap**

Leaving out the 5 × 5 square (a square *is* a rectangle) and answering 24 − 9 = 15 cm², or counting 3 × 7 and 7 × 3 as two different rectangles.

questions.title: Folded in half
questions.stem:
A square sheet of paper is folded exactly in half along the dashed line to make a rectangle. The perimeter of the folded rectangle is 30 cm.

What was the area of the original square sheet?

![A square sheet with a dashed fold line across its middle, and the rectangle formed after folding it in half.](asset:q8-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The folded rectangle is one full side of the square long and half a side wide. Its boundary is two full sides plus two half sides — exactly *three* sides of the square.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Folding in half keeps the full width of the square and halves its height.
2. Perimeter of the rectangle = side + side + half side + half side = 3 sides of the square.
3. 3 sides = 30 cm, so one side of the square is 30 ÷ 3 = 10 cm.
4. Area of the original square = 10 × 10 = 100 cm².

**Calculation**

- rectangle = side × (half a side)
- perimeter = 2 sides + 2 half-sides = 3 sides = 30 cm
- side = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 cm
- area = 10 × 10 = 100 cm²  (check: 2 × (10 + 5) = 30 cm)

**Why the method works**

Measuring the boundary in “sides of the square” turns the fold into a counting problem. Folding halves the area, but it does not halve the perimeter.

**Common trap**

Assuming the perimeter halves when the paper is folded: doubling 30 cm to 60 cm gives a side of 15 cm and a wrong area of 225 cm².

questions.title: Tiles of unknown size
questions.stem:
A rectangle is made from 24 identical square tiles arranged in 4 rows of 6 tiles, as shown. The perimeter of the rectangle is 40 cm.

What is the area of the rectangle?

![A rectangle made of 24 identical square tiles in 4 rows of 6. No lengths are marked.](asset:q9-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Measure the boundary in tile edges: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 tile edges make the 40 cm perimeter.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Along the top and bottom there are 6 tile edges each; along each end there are 4. The boundary is 20 tile edges.
2. 20 tile edges = 40 cm, so one tile edge is 40 ÷ 20 = 2 cm.
3. Each tile has area 2 × 2 = 4 cm².
4. Area of the rectangle = 24 × 4 = 96 cm². (Check: it is 12 cm by 8 cm, and 12 × 8 = 96.)

**Calculation**

- boundary = 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 tile edges
- tile edge = 40 ÷ 20 = 2 cm
- area = 24 × (2 × 2) = 96 cm²
- check: 12 × 8 = 96 cm²

**Why the method works**

Only edges on the outside count towards the perimeter, and each is one tile side. Once the tile side is known, the area follows from the number of tiles or from the rectangle’s length and width.

**Common trap**

Answering 24 cm² by assuming each tile is 1 cm by 1 cm. A tile is one square centimetre only if its side is 1 cm.

questions.title: Three strips make a square
questions.stem:
A square is cut into three identical rectangular strips by two straight cuts parallel to one of its sides, as shown. Each strip has a perimeter of 24 cm.

What is the area of the square?

![A square divided into three identical vertical strips. No lengths are marked.](asset:q10-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Let the width of a strip be 1 part. The square’s side is 3 strip-widths, so each strip is 3 parts long and 1 part wide.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Three identical strips fill the square, so a strip is one third as wide as the square and as long as the square’s side.
2. Call the strip’s width 1 part; its length is then 3 parts.
3. Perimeter of a strip = 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 8 parts = 24 cm, so 1 part = 3 cm.
4. The square’s side = 3 parts = 9 cm, so its area is 9 × 9 = 81 cm².

**Calculation**

- strip = 3 parts × 1 part
- perimeter = 8 parts = 24 cm  →  1 part = 3 cm
- square side = 9 cm
- area = 9 × 9 = 81 cm²

**Why the method works**

Writing every length in the same unit (“parts”) turns the shape’s structure into a simple division. This is the bar-model method used in Olympiad problems.

**Common trap**

Treating a strip like a square (24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm), or assuming the square’s perimeter is 3 × 24 = 72 cm. The cuts are inside the square, so they are not part of its perimeter.

questions.title: Seven identical tiles
questions.stem:
Seven identical rectangles fit together exactly, with no gaps or overlaps, to form a large rectangle. In the top row two of them lie end to end with their long sides horizontal; in the bottom row five of them stand side by side with their long sides vertical.

The perimeter of the large rectangle is 34 cm. Find the area of one small rectangle.

![Seven identical rectangles: two lying end to end in the top row and five standing side by side in the bottom row, together forming a large rectangle.](asset:q11-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The top row and the bottom row are both exactly as wide as the large rectangle. So *2 long sides = 5 short sides*.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Top row width = 2 long sides. Bottom row width = 5 short sides. Both equal the width of the large rectangle, so 2 long sides = 5 short sides.
2. Use “parts”: if a short side is 2 parts, then 2 long sides are 10 parts, so a long side is 5 parts.
3. Large rectangle: width = 2 long sides = 10 parts; height = 1 short side + 1 long side = 2 + 5 = 7 parts.
4. Perimeter = 2 × (10 + 7) = 34 parts = 34 cm, so 1 part = 1 cm.
5. A small rectangle is 5 cm by 2 cm, so its area is 10 cm².

**Calculation**

- 2 × long = 5 × short  →  short = 2 parts, long = 5 parts
- large: 10 parts × 7 parts
- perimeter = 2 × (10 + 7) = 34 parts = 34 cm  →  1 part = 1 cm
- area = 5 × 2 = 10 cm²

**Why the method works**

Two different routes across the same rectangle must have the same length. That equation fixes the *shape* of the small rectangle; the perimeter then fixes its *size*.

**Common trap**

Guessing that a small rectangle is “twice as long as it is wide” because it looks that way. The drawing only shows how the pieces are arranged; the 2 : 5 relationship must come from the rows.

questions.title: Three equal areas
questions.stem:
A rectangle 12 cm long and 10 cm high is divided into three smaller rectangles P, Q and R with **equal areas**. Piece P runs the full height on the left; the space to its right is cut by a horizontal line into Q and R.

![A 12 cm by 10 cm rectangle divided into a tall piece P on the left and two pieces Q and R stacked on the right.](asset:q12-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of P.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the perimeters of Q and R.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Equal areas plus a shared side force the other sides to match: P’s height is known (10 cm), and Q and R share a width.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Total area = 12 × 10 = 120 cm², so each piece has area 120 ÷ 3 = 40 cm².
2. P is 10 cm high, so its width is 40 ÷ 10 = 4 cm. (a) Perimeter of P = 2 × (4 + 10) = 28 cm.
3. The right-hand part is 12 − 4 = 8 cm wide. Q and R are both 8 cm wide with area 40 cm², so each is 40 ÷ 8 = 5 cm high (and 5 + 5 = 10 ✓).
4. (b) Perimeter of Q = perimeter of R = 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 cm.

**Calculation**

- each area = 120 ÷ 3 = 40 cm²
- P: 40 ÷ 10 = 4 cm wide  →  2 × (4 + 10) = 28 cm
- Q, R: 8 cm wide, 40 ÷ 8 = 5 cm high  →  2 × (8 + 5) = 26 cm

**Why the method works**

Area = width × height, so when the area and one side of a rectangle are known, the other side is a division away. Equal areas did *not* give equal perimeters: P is thinner, so its boundary is longer.

**Common trap**

Splitting the 12 cm length into three equal 4 cm parts for all three pieces, or assuming that equal areas mean equal perimeters.

questions.title: Pinwheel around a hole
questions.stem:
Four identical rectangles are arranged around a square hole so that together they form a large square, as shown.

The large square has an area of 100 cm² and the square hole has an area of 16 cm².

![Four identical rectangles arranged like a pinwheel around a square hole, forming a large square.](asset:q13-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of one rectangle.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the area of one rectangle.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Along each side of the large square you see one *long* side of one rectangle followed by one *short* side of the next. So long + short = side of the large square.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Area of the large square is 100 cm², so its side is 10 cm.
2. The top edge is made of the long side of the top rectangle and the short side of the right-hand rectangle. All four rectangles are identical, so for each one: long side + short side = 10 cm.
3. (a) Perimeter of one rectangle = 2 × (long + short) = 2 × 10 = 20 cm. The hole is not needed for this part.
4. (b) The four rectangles cover the large square except the hole: 100 − 16 = 84 cm², so one rectangle has 84 ÷ 4 = 21 cm².
5. Check: the hole’s side (4 cm) equals long − short. Long + short = 10 and long − short = 4 give 7 cm and 3 cm, and 7 × 3 = 21 ✓.

**Calculation**

- large side = 10 cm (10 × 10 = 100)
- long + short = 10  →  perimeter = 2 × 10 = 20 cm
- area of four rectangles = 100 − 16 = 84 cm²  →  one = 21 cm²
- check: 7 + 3 = 10, 7 − 3 = 4, 7 × 3 = 21

**Why the method works**

Reading the side of the big square as “one long + one short” turns the picture into a fact about a single rectangle. Subtracting the hole from the big square counts exactly the four rectangles.

**Common trap**

Taking the long side of a rectangle to be the whole side of the large square (10 cm). The long side stops where the next rectangle begins.

questions.title: Double trouble
questions.stem:
The length and the width of a rectangle are both doubled. The new rectangle has a perimeter of 56 cm and an area of 192 cm².

Find the length and the width of the original rectangle.

![A small original rectangle next to a larger rectangle whose length and width are both twice as long. No lengths are marked.](asset:q14-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Doubling both sides *doubles* the perimeter, but four copies of the original fit inside the new rectangle (2 along × 2 up), so the area is multiplied by *4*.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Every side doubles, so the perimeter doubles: original perimeter = 56 ÷ 2 = 28 cm, so length + width = 14 cm.
2. The new rectangle can be split into 2 × 2 = 4 copies of the original, so original area = 192 ÷ 4 = 48 cm².
3. Find two numbers that add to 14 and multiply to 48: 7 & 7 give 49, 8 & 6 give 48 ✓, 9 & 5 give 45, and the products keep falling as the numbers spread further apart.
4. The original rectangle is 8 cm long and 6 cm wide.
5. Check: doubled it is 16 cm by 12 cm: perimeter 2 × (16 + 12) = 56 cm and area 16 × 12 = 192 cm² ✓.

**Calculation**

- original perimeter = 56 ÷ 2 = 28  →  length + width = 14
- original area = 192 ÷ 4 = 48
- 8 + 6 = 14 and 8 × 6 = 48
- check: 16 × 12 = 192, 2 × (16 + 12) = 56

**Why the method works**

Perimeter is a length, so it scales like the sides (× 2). Area counts squares in two directions, so it scales twice (× 2 × 2 = × 4). For pairs adding to 14, the product is 49 minus the square of how far each number is from 7, so only 8 and 6 give 48.

**Common trap**

Halving the area as well as the perimeter. That gives 96 cm², but no two numbers adding to 14 multiply to 96 — a sign that something went wrong.

questions.title: How long is the cut?
questions.stem:
A rectangle is cut into two smaller rectangles P and Q by one straight line parallel to its shorter sides. Rectangle P has a perimeter of 30 cm and rectangle Q has a perimeter of 40 cm. The original rectangle had a perimeter of 54 cm.

![A rectangle cut by one line parallel to its shorter sides into a smaller rectangle P and a larger rectangle Q. No lengths are marked.](asset:q15-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long is the cut?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: What were the length and width of the original rectangle?

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The perimeters of the two pieces together are the original perimeter *plus the cut twice*, because the cut is a side of both pieces.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. P and Q together: 30 + 40 = 70 cm of boundary.
2. The original boundary is 54 cm; the extra 70 − 54 = 16 cm is the cut counted twice. (a) The cut is 16 ÷ 2 = 8 cm.
3. The cut runs straight across between the two long sides, so it is as long as the width: the width is 8 cm.
4. (b) 2 × (length + 8) = 54, so length + 8 = 27 and the length is 19 cm.
5. Check: P is 7 cm by 8 cm (2 × 15 = 30 ✓), Q is 12 cm by 8 cm (2 × 20 = 40 ✓), and 7 + 12 = 19 ✓.

**Calculation**

- 70 − 54 = 16 = 2 × cut  →  cut = 8 cm
- width = 8 cm
- 54 ÷ 2 = 27  →  length = 27 − 8 = 19 cm
- check: 7 + 12 = 19

**Why the method works**

Cutting never changes the total area, but it always adds the cut twice to the total boundary. Using that fact backwards finds the cut without knowing where it was made.

**Common trap**

Expecting 30 + 40 to equal 54 and concluding the problem is impossible, or forgetting that a cut parallel to the shorter sides has the same length as the width.

questions.title: Four rooms, three perimeters
questions.stem:
A rectangle is divided into four smaller rectangles by one straight vertical line and one straight horizontal line, each running right across it. The perimeters of three of the small rectangles are written inside them.

![A rectangle divided by one vertical and one horizontal line into four smaller rectangles; three of them are labelled with their perimeters 20 cm (top left), 26 cm (top right) and 24 cm (bottom left); the bottom right one is marked with a question mark.](asset:q16-fig1)

*Not to scale. The numbers inside the rooms are perimeters.*

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the fourth rectangle (marked ?).

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Can the *area* of the fourth rectangle be found from this information? Explain.
parts.answer: No. For example, 7 cm × 8 cm = 56 cm² and 6 cm × 9 cm = 54 cm² both fit every clue.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The top-left and bottom-right rooms together use one of each width and one of each height. So do the top-right and bottom-left rooms. Their perimeter totals must therefore be equal.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Call the two widths “left width” and “right width”, and the two heights “top height” and “bottom height”.
2. Top-left + bottom-right perimeters = 2 × (left width + top height) + 2 × (right width + bottom height).
3. Top-right + bottom-left perimeters = 2 × (right width + top height) + 2 × (left width + bottom height) — the very same four lengths, each doubled.
4. (a) So 20 + ? = 26 + 24 = 50, and ? = 30 cm.
5. (b) Try left width 4, top height 6: then right width 7, bottom height 8, and the fourth room is 7 × 8 = 56 cm². Try left width 3, top height 7: then right width 6, bottom height 9, and the fourth room is 6 × 9 = 54 cm². Both fit every clue, so the area is **not** determined.
6. One actual length (for example, the left width) would fix every length, and then the area.

**Calculation**

- 20 + ? = 26 + 24
- ? = 50 − 20 = 30 cm
- case 1: 2(4+6)=20, 2(7+6)=26, 2(4+8)=24, area 7 × 8 = 56
- case 2: 2(3+7)=20, 2(6+7)=26, 2(3+9)=24, area 6 × 9 = 54

**Why the method works**

The sum of the perimeters of two diagonally opposite rooms always uses each of the four lengths exactly twice, so it is the same for both diagonal pairs. Perimeter clues fix sums of lengths, not the lengths themselves, which is why the area stays open.

**Common trap**

Assuming the lines cut the sides in half, or reasoning that “if the perimeter is known, the area must be known too”.

questions.title: Pen against a wall
questions.stem:
A farmer has 24 m of fencing to make a rectangular pen against a long straight wall. The wall forms one side of the pen, so the fence is needed on the other three sides only. The sides of the pen are whole numbers of metres.

What is the largest possible area of the pen, and what are its length and width?

![A rectangular pen against a straight wall. A dashed fence runs along the three sides that are not against the wall.](asset:q17-fig1)

*One possible pen is drawn (not the answer).*
questions.answer: 72 m², with the pen 12 m long (along the wall) and 6 m wide

solution.answer: 72 m², with the pen 12 m long (along the wall) and 6 m wide
solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The fence covers only three sides. The best pen is *not* a square: its side along the wall should be twice each side going out from the wall.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Let each side going out from the wall be *w* m. The side parallel to the wall uses the rest of the fence: 24 − 2*w* m.
2. Make a table: w = 3 → 18 × 3 = 54; w = 4 → 16 × 4 = 64; w = 5 → 14 × 5 = 70; w = 6 → 12 × 6 = 72; w = 7 → 10 × 7 = 70; w = 8 → 8 × 8 = 64.
3. The areas rise and then fall; the largest is 72 m² when w = 6.
4. So the pen is 12 m along the wall and 6 m out from it: 6 + 12 + 6 = 24 m of fence ✓.

**Calculation**

- fence: w + (24 − 2w) + w = 24
- w = 5: 14 × 5 = 70
- w = 6: 12 × 6 = 72  ← largest
- w = 7: 10 × 7 = 70

**Why the method works**

Imagine the wall is a mirror. The pen and its reflection form a rectangle fenced by 48 m all round, and a fixed perimeter encloses the most area when the rectangle is a square, 12 m by 12 m. The real pen is half of that square: 12 m by 6 m.

**Common trap**

Making the pen a square (8 m × 8 m gives only 64 m²), or treating 24 m as the perimeter of all four sides (a 6 m × 6 m square, 36 m²) — the wall side needs no fence.

questions.title: Two ways to join four rectangles
questions.stem:
Four identical rectangles can be joined in two ways. In arrangement P they stand side by side in one row, long sides touching. In arrangement Q they form a 2 by 2 block.

Arrangement P has a perimeter of 44 cm and arrangement Q has a perimeter of 40 cm. Find the area of one rectangle.

![Arrangement P: four identical upright rectangles side by side in a row. Arrangement Q: the same four rectangles in a 2 by 2 block.](asset:q18-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Half of each perimeter can be counted in sides of the small rectangle. Q gives 2 short + 2 long; P gives 4 short + 1 long — the difference is made only of short sides.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. P: half the perimeter = 4 short sides (across) + 1 long side (up) = 44 ÷ 2 = 22 cm.
2. Q: half the perimeter = 2 short sides (across) + 2 long sides (up) = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 cm, so 1 short + 1 long = 10 cm.
3. P’s 22 cm = (1 short + 1 long) + 3 short = 10 + 3 short, so 3 short sides = 12 cm and a short side is 4 cm.
4. The long side is 10 − 4 = 6 cm, so one rectangle has area 4 × 6 = 24 cm².
5. Check: P is 16 cm by 6 cm (perimeter 44 ✓); Q is 8 cm by 12 cm (perimeter 40 ✓).

**Calculation**

- P: 4 short + 1 long = 22
- Q: 2 short + 2 long = 20  →  1 short + 1 long = 10
- 22 − 10 = 12 = 3 short  →  short = 4 cm, long = 6 cm
- area = 4 × 6 = 24 cm²

**Why the method works**

Each arrangement turns its perimeter into a “sides count”. Comparing two counts that share a common chunk (1 short + 1 long) isolates one unknown at a time — no guessing needed.

**Common trap**

Adding up the perimeters of the four separate rectangles (the shared edges are not on the outside), or assuming the rectangles are twice as long as they are wide.

questions.title: Squares on every side
questions.stem:
A rectangle has a perimeter of 22 cm. On each of its four sides a square is drawn outwards, using that whole side of the rectangle as one side of the square.

![A rectangle with a square drawn outwards on each of its four sides, making a cross-like figure.](asset:q19-fig1)

*One possible rectangle is drawn.*

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the whole figure (the rectangle and the four squares together).

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Can the total area of the figure be found from this information? Explain.
parts.answer: No. A 7 cm × 4 cm rectangle gives 158 cm², but a 6 cm × 5 cm rectangle gives 152 cm².

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Each square hides one side of the rectangle and adds its other *three* sides to the outline. So the outline is three of each rectangle side: 3 × (the rectangle’s perimeter).

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. The side a square shares with the rectangle is inside the figure. Its other three sides are on the outside.
2. The two squares on the long sides add 3 × length each; the two on the short sides add 3 × width each.
3. Outline = 3 × (length + length + width + width) = 3 × 22 = 66 cm. (At each corner of the rectangle two squares meet only at a point, so nothing else is on the outside.) (a) 66 cm.
4. (b) We only know length + width = 11 cm. If the rectangle is 7 × 4: area = 28 + 2 × 49 + 2 × 16 = 158 cm². If it is 6 × 5: area = 30 + 2 × 36 + 2 × 25 = 152 cm².
5. Two different answers fit the facts, so the area cannot be found. Knowing the length (or the width) would settle it.

**Calculation**

- outline = 3 × perimeter of rectangle = 3 × 22 = 66 cm
- 7 × 4: 28 + 98 + 32 = 158 cm²
- 6 × 5: 30 + 72 + 50 = 152 cm²

**Why the method works**

Perimeter here depends only on the *sum* length + width, which is fixed. Area depends on the actual lengths, which are not fixed. The same picture gives one perimeter but many areas.

**Common trap**

Counting all four sides of each square (88 cm), or adding the rectangle’s own perimeter to the squares’ outer sides.

questions.title: When area equals perimeter
questions.stem:
In the rectangle drawn on the 1 cm grid, the area is 10 cm² but the perimeter is 14 cm, so the two numbers do not match.

Find **every** rectangle with whole-number sides (in cm) whose area, in cm², is the same number as its perimeter, in cm. Explain why there are no others.

![A 5 cm by 2 cm rectangle drawn on a 1 centimetre grid.](asset:q20-fig1)
questions.answer: Exactly two: 3 cm × 6 cm (area 18 cm², perimeter 18 cm) and 4 cm × 4 cm (area 16 cm², perimeter 16 cm).

solution.answer: Exactly two: 3 cm × 6 cm (area 18 cm², perimeter 18 cm) and 4 cm × 4 cm (area 16 cm², perimeter 16 cm).
solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Compare how the two numbers grow. Making the rectangle 1 cm longer adds *width* cm² to the area but only 2 cm to the perimeter.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Let the width be the shorter side. Check widths one at a time.
2. Width 1: area = length, perimeter = 2 × length + 2 — always bigger. No solutions.
3. Width 2: area = 2 × length, perimeter = 2 × length + 4 — always 4 bigger. No solutions.
4. Width 3: area = 3 × length, perimeter = 2 × length + 6. They match when the extra length equals 6: length 6. Rectangle 3 × 6.
5. Width 4: area = 4 × length, perimeter = 2 × length + 8. They match when 2 × length = 8: length 4. Rectangle 4 × 4.
6. Width 5 or more: the length is at least the width, so perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width ≤ 4 × length, while area ≥ 5 × length. The area is always bigger. No more solutions.

**Calculation**

- 3 × 6 = 18 and 2 × (3 + 6) = 18
- 4 × 4 = 16 and 2 × (4 + 4) = 16
- width ≥ 5: perimeter ≤ 4 × length \< 5 × length ≤ area

**Why the method works**

Fixing the width turns the problem into comparing two simple growth patterns. For wide rectangles the area races ahead of the perimeter, which proves the list is complete.

**Common trap**

Stopping after finding 4 × 4 (or 3 × 6), or testing a few sizes without explaining why larger widths can never work.

questions.title: An L with two silent sides
questions.stem:
All the corners of this L-shaped figure are right angles. Four of its six sides are marked.

![An L-shaped figure with right-angled corners. Marked: top 4 cm, left 8 cm, bottom 10 cm, short right side 3 cm. Two inner sides are unmarked.](asset:q21-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the figure.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find its area.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The unmarked sides are hidden in the marked ones: the two top-facing horizontal sides together match the 10 cm bottom, and the two right-facing vertical sides together match the 8 cm left side.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Unmarked horizontal side = 10 − 4 = 6 cm (the top of the figure must span the same 10 cm as the bottom).
2. Unmarked vertical side = 8 − 3 = 5 cm (the right-hand sides must drop the same 8 cm as the left side).
3. (a) Perimeter = 4 + 5 + 6 + 3 + 10 + 8 = 36 cm — exactly the perimeter of a 10 cm by 8 cm rectangle.
4. (b) Cut the figure with a vertical line: a 4 × 8 piece (32 cm²) and a 6 × 3 piece (18 cm²). Area = 50 cm².
5. Check the area another way: 10 × 8 − 6 × 5 = 80 − 30 = 50 cm².

**Calculation**

- 10 − 4 = 6 cm,  8 − 3 = 5 cm
- perimeter = 4 + 5 + 6 + 3 + 10 + 8 = 36 cm = 2 × (10 + 8)
- area = 4 × 8 + 6 × 3 = 32 + 18 = 50 cm²
- check: 80 − 30 = 50 cm²

**Why the method works**

Pushing the two inner sides outwards turns the L into its surrounding 10 × 8 rectangle without changing the total length of horizontal or vertical edges, so the perimeter stays the same. The area, however, does change — the missing corner really is missing.

**Common trap**

Adding only the four marked sides (25 cm), or giving the area as 10 × 8 = 80 cm². Equal perimeters do not mean equal areas.

questions.title: A bite from the middle
questions.stem:
A 4 cm by 3 cm rectangular piece is cut out of the middle of the top edge of a 12 cm by 7 cm rectangle, without touching a corner, as shown.

![A 12 cm by 7 cm rectangle with a 4 cm wide, 3 cm deep rectangular notch cut from the middle of its top edge. The removed piece is shown dashed.](asset:q22-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter and the area of the shape that remains.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: If the same 4 cm by 3 cm piece had been cut from a *corner* instead, what would the perimeter of the remaining shape have been?

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

A notch in the middle of an edge removes 4 cm of edge but creates 3 + 4 + 3 = 10 cm of new edge: the perimeter grows by twice the depth. At a corner, the new edges exactly replace the old ones.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Original perimeter = 2 × (12 + 7) = 38 cm.
2. The middle notch takes away 4 cm of the top edge and adds its two 3 cm sides and its 4 cm bottom: change = −4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = +6 cm.
3. (a) Perimeter = 38 + 6 = 44 cm. Area = 12 × 7 − 4 × 3 = 84 − 12 = 72 cm².
4. (b) At a corner, the cut removes 4 cm of the top edge and 3 cm of the side edge, and adds a new 3 cm edge and a new 4 cm edge: change = 0. The perimeter stays 38 cm.

**Calculation**

- 38 − 4 + (3 + 4 + 3) = 44 cm
- 84 − 12 = 72 cm²
- corner: 38 − 4 − 3 + 3 + 4 = 38 cm

**Why the method works**

Only the edges that face the outside count. A corner notch just moves two edges inwards (same lengths), while a middle notch adds two brand-new sides going down into the shape.

**Common trap**

Believing that cutting a piece away must make the perimeter smaller. Here the area goes down but the perimeter goes up.

questions.title: A tower on a base
questions.stem:
A square of side 3 cm is placed on top of a 10 cm by 4 cm rectangle so that the whole bottom side of the square lies along the top side of the rectangle, away from its ends.

Find the perimeter and the area of the combined shape.

![A 10 cm by 4 cm rectangle with a 3 cm square standing on its top side, away from the ends.](asset:q23-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Where the two shapes meet, a 3 cm edge disappears from *both* outlines, so 2 × 3 cm must be taken away from the sum of the two perimeters.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Perimeter of the rectangle = 2 × (10 + 4) = 28 cm; perimeter of the square = 4 × 3 = 12 cm. Together: 40 cm.
2. The bottom of the square (3 cm) and the 3 cm of the rectangle’s top underneath it are now inside the shape: remove 2 × 3 = 6 cm.
3. Perimeter = 40 − 6 = 34 cm.
4. Area = 10 × 4 + 3 × 3 = 40 + 9 = 49 cm².
5. Check: the shape is 10 cm wide and 4 + 3 = 7 cm tall, and every horizontal or vertical line meets it in one piece, so its perimeter equals that of a 10 × 7 rectangle: 2 × 17 = 34 cm ✓.

**Calculation**

- 28 + 12 = 40 cm
- 40 − 2 × 3 = 34 cm
- area = 40 + 9 = 49 cm²
- check: 2 × (10 + 7) = 34 cm

**Why the method works**

Perimeter counts edges with the outside on one side only. The joined 3 cm edges have shape on both sides, so they are not boundary any more.

**Common trap**

Adding 28 + 12 = 40 cm without removing anything, or removing the shared 3 cm only once (37 cm).

questions.title: Photo on a card
questions.stem:
A rectangular photo 12 cm long and 8 cm wide is glued onto a rectangular card so that a border 2 cm wide shows all the way round.

![A 12 cm by 8 cm photo on a card, with a 2 cm border showing all round.](asset:q24-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the card.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the area of the border.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The border shows on *both* ends of every side, so each dimension of the card is 2 + 2 = 4 cm longer than the photo, not 2 cm.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Card length = 2 + 12 + 2 = 16 cm; card width = 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 cm.
2. (a) Perimeter of the card = 2 × (16 + 12) = 56 cm.
3. Area of card = 16 × 12 = 192 cm²; area of photo = 12 × 8 = 96 cm².
4. (b) Border = 192 − 96 = 96 cm².
5. Check by pieces: top and bottom strips 16 × 2 each (64 cm²) plus two side strips 2 × 8 each (32 cm²) = 96 cm² ✓.

**Calculation**

- card = 16 cm × 12 cm
- perimeter = 2 × (16 + 12) = 56 cm
- border = 192 − 96 = 96 cm²
- check: 2 × 32 + 2 × 16 = 96 cm²

**Why the method works**

The border is “card minus photo”. Splitting it into four strips without overlapping the corners gives an independent check.

**Common trap**

Adding 2 cm only once to each side (a 14 × 10 card), which gives a perimeter of 48 cm and a border of 44 cm².

questions.title: The plus sign and the missing middle
questions.stem:
Five identical squares of side 4 cm form the plus sign in picture (a).

![Picture (a): five 4 cm squares forming a plus sign. Picture (b): the same shape with the middle square removed, so four squares meet only at corners.](asset:q25-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the plus sign.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: The middle square is now removed, as in picture (b). The four squares that are left touch only at their corners. Find the total length of the boundary of what is left.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

In the plus sign, each outer square hides one side against the middle square, and the middle square hides all four of its sides. Removing the middle square *uncovers* four hidden edges.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. (a) Each of the four arm squares has 3 sides on the outside; the middle square has none. That is 4 × 3 = 12 sides of 4 cm: 48 cm.
2. (b) Without the middle square, no two squares share an edge (they meet only at points), so all 4 sides of each of the 4 squares are boundary: 16 sides of 4 cm = 64 cm.
3. The area went down from 80 cm² to 64 cm², yet the boundary went up from 48 cm to 64 cm.

**Calculation**

- (a) 12 sides × 4 cm = 48 cm
- (b) 16 sides × 4 cm = 64 cm
- areas: 5 × 16 = 80 cm²  →  4 × 16 = 64 cm²

**Why the method works**

A side is on the boundary exactly when there is no square on its other side. Removing the middle square leaves nothing on the other side of four edges, so they become boundary.

**Common trap**

Assuming that removing a piece must shorten the boundary, or counting 4 sides per square in (a) (80 cm).

questions.title: A frame from two perimeters
questions.stem:
A square frame is made by cutting a smaller square out of the centre of a square card, leaving a border of the same width all the way round.

The outer edge of the frame measures 40 cm all round, and the inner edge (round the hole) measures 24 cm all round.

![A square frame: a square card with a smaller square hole in the centre, leaving an equal border all round. No lengths are marked.](asset:q26-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How wide is the frame?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: What is the area of the frame?

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Across the card you cross the border *twice* — once on each side of the hole — so the outer side = border + hole side + border.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Outer side = 40 ÷ 4 = 10 cm; inner side = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm.
2. 10 cm = border + 6 cm + border, so two borders make 4 cm. (a) The frame is 2 cm wide.
3. (b) Area of frame = 10 × 10 − 6 × 6 = 100 − 36 = 64 cm².
4. Check: the frame can be cut into four identical 8 cm × 2 cm strips arranged like a pinwheel: 4 × 16 = 64 cm² ✓.

**Calculation**

- outer side 10 cm, inner side 6 cm
- 10 − 6 = 4 = 2 × width  →  width = 2 cm
- area = 100 − 36 = 64 cm²

**Why the method works**

Working backwards from each perimeter gives each side. The difference of the sides is shared between the two sides of the hole.

**Common trap**

Taking the width as 10 − 6 = 4 cm (forgetting the border is on both sides), or subtracting the perimeters (40 − 24 = 16) and calling that an area.

questions.title: Crossed rectangles
questions.stem:
Two identical rectangles, each 10 cm by 4 cm, cross at right angles to make a plus shape. Each rectangle sticks out 3 cm beyond the other on both sides, as shown.

![Two identical 10 cm by 4 cm rectangles crossing at right angles to form a plus shape; the square where they overlap is shaded darker. Each arm sticks out 3 cm.](asset:q27-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the area of the plus shape.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find its perimeter.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The overlap is a 4 cm square that belongs to both rectangles: it is counted twice in the areas, and the parts of each outline inside it are not on the boundary.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Each rectangle is 4 cm wide, so the overlap is a 4 cm by 4 cm square.
2. (a) Area = 40 + 40 − 16 = 64 cm² (the overlap was counted twice).
3. (b) The shape has four arms. Each arm sticks out 3 cm and is 4 cm wide, so its outside edges are 3 + 4 + 3 = 10 cm. Four arms: 40 cm.
4. Check: two outlines total 28 + 28 = 56 cm. Inside the overlap lie 4 cm of the top and 4 cm of the bottom of the horizontal rectangle, and 4 cm of each long side of the vertical one: 16 cm. 56 − 16 = 40 cm ✓.

**Calculation**

- overlap = 4 × 4 = 16 cm²
- area = 40 + 40 − 16 = 64 cm²
- perimeter = 4 arms × (3 + 4 + 3) = 40 cm
- check: 56 − 16 = 40 cm

**Why the method works**

Adding the two rectangles counts the shared square twice, so it is subtracted once. For the perimeter, only edges with the outside on one side count, and none of the edges inside the overlap do.

**Common trap**

Adding the two perimeters (56 cm) or adding the two areas (80 cm²) without allowing for the overlap.

questions.title: Counting shared edges
questions.stem:
This shape is made of 10 squares, each of side 2 cm, joined edge to edge.

![A staircase-like shape made of 10 equal squares on a square grid; one square side is marked 2 cm.](asset:q28-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the shape.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: One more 2 cm square is to be added, sharing one or more whole sides with the shape. What is the smallest possible perimeter of the new shape?
parts.answer: 36 cm (the perimeter need not grow at all)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Every square brings 4 sides, and every place where two squares touch hides 2 sides (one from each). So: boundary sides = 4 × (number of squares) − 2 × (number of shared edges).

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Count the shared edges: in the rows, 2 + 2 + 2 = 6; in the columns, 1 + 2 + 2 = 5. Total 11 shared edges.
2. Boundary sides = 4 × 10 − 2 × 11 = 40 − 22 = 18 sides.
3. (a) Perimeter = 18 × 2 cm = 36 cm.
4. (b) A new square adds 4 sides and hides 2 sides for every edge it shares. Sharing 1 edge: +4 − 2 = +2 sides. Sharing 2 edges: +4 − 4 = 0.
5. There are inside corners where a new square touches two squares at once (for example, to the left of the bottom square of the second column of the staircase). No empty square touches three. So the smallest new perimeter is still 18 sides = 36 cm.

**Calculation**

- shared edges = 6 + 5 = 11
- boundary = 40 − 22 = 18 sides = 36 cm
- new square sharing 2 edges: 18 + 4 − 4 = 18 sides = 36 cm

**Why the method works**

Each shared edge is inside the shape, with a square on both sides. Counting shared edges instead of tracing the outline avoids missing a step in a complicated boundary.

**Common trap**

Counting the outside edges by eye and missing some of the steps, or forgetting to multiply the number of sides by 2 cm.

questions.title: Paths through a garden
questions.stem:
A rectangular garden 20 m long and 12 m wide is crossed by two straight paths, each 2 m wide: one parallel to the length and one parallel to the width. Neither path runs along an edge of the garden, but their exact positions are *not* given. The rest of the garden is grass, in four rectangles.

![A 20 m by 12 m garden crossed by two 2 m wide paths, one running across and one running down, dividing the grass into four rectangles.](asset:q29-fig1)

*The paths may be anywhere, as long as they cross the garden away from its edges.*

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the total area of grass.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the total of the perimeters of the four grass rectangles.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Slide the four grass pieces together to close up the paths: they fit into one rectangle 2 m shorter in each direction, wherever the paths were.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Closing the paths removes 2 m from the length and 2 m from the width: the grass fits together as an 18 m by 10 m rectangle.
2. (a) Grass area = 18 × 10 = 180 m².
3. The two left pieces have the same width, and so do the two right pieces; those two widths add to 18 m. Likewise the top height and bottom height add to 10 m.
4. Each grass piece has perimeter 2 × (its width + its height). Over all four pieces, each width appears in two pieces and each height in two pieces.
5. (b) Total = 2 × 2 × (18 + 10) = 112 m. For the drawn positions: 2(7+4) + 2(11+4) + 2(7+6) + 2(11+6) = 22 + 30 + 26 + 34 = 112 ✓.

**Calculation**

- grass = (20 − 2) × (12 − 2) = 18 × 10 = 180 m²
- total perimeter = 4 × 18 + 4 × 10 = 112 m

**Why the method works**

Sliding pieces without turning or overlapping keeps their areas, so the grass area is the area of the closed-up rectangle. The total perimeter depends only on the sums of the widths and heights, which are fixed.

**Common trap**

Subtracting the path areas: 240 − 40 − 24 = 176 m². The 2 m by 2 m crossing square belongs to both paths and has been subtracted twice.

questions.title: A step pyramid of squares
questions.stem:
Four squares with sides 2 cm, 4 cm, 6 cm and 8 cm stand in a row on a straight line, in that order, each touching the next with no gap.

![Four squares of sides 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm standing side by side on a line, growing from left to right like steps.](asset:q30-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the whole shape.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find its area.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Because the steps only go up, the top-facing edges add to the full width, and the rising edges add to the full height: the perimeter equals that of the surrounding 20 cm by 8 cm rectangle.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Width of the shape = 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20 cm; height = 8 cm (the tallest square).
2. Horizontal edges: the bottom is 20 cm, and the top edges of the four squares together are also 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20 cm.
3. Vertical edges: the right side drops 8 cm; going up from the left, the left side and the three rises are 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 cm.
4. (a) Perimeter = 20 + 20 + 8 + 8 = 56 cm.
5. (b) Area = 4 + 16 + 36 + 64 = 120 cm².

**Calculation**

- horizontal: 20 + 20 = 40 cm
- vertical: 8 + 8 = 16 cm
- perimeter = 56 cm = 2 × (20 + 8)
- area = 2² + 4² + 6² + 8² = 120 cm²

**Why the method works**

Moving each step’s edges outward to the surrounding rectangle changes no lengths, so the staircase and the rectangle have equal perimeters. Their areas are different (120 cm² against 160 cm²).

**Common trap**

Adding the four squares’ perimeters (80 cm) without removing the hidden shared parts, or using the area of the surrounding rectangle (160 cm²).

questions.title: Three bites

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Judge each bite separately: a corner bite leaves the perimeter unchanged; a bite in the middle of an edge adds *twice its depth*.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Original perimeter = 2 × (16 + 10) = 52 cm; original area = 160 cm².
2. Bite A (corner): removes 3 + 3 cm of outer edge and creates two new edges of 3 cm and 3 cm. Change: 0.
3. Bite B (middle of an edge): removes 2 cm of the bottom edge and adds 4 + 2 + 4 = 10 cm. Change: +8 cm (twice the depth 4).
4. Bite C (middle of an edge): removes 3 cm of the right edge and adds 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 cm. Change: +4 cm (twice the depth 2).
5. Perimeter = 52 + 0 + 8 + 4 = 64 cm.
6. Area = 160 − 9 − 8 − 6 = 137 cm².

**Calculation**

- 52 + 0 + 2 × 4 + 2 × 2 = 64 cm
- 160 − 3 × 3 − 2 × 4 − 3 × 2 = 160 − 23 = 137 cm²

**Why the method works**

The width of a middle bite is replaced by an equal edge at its bottom, so only its two sides are extra. A corner bite simply moves two edges inwards without changing their lengths.

**Common trap**

Subtracting something from the perimeter for every bite, or adding each bite’s full perimeter.

questions.title: Two squares overlapping at a corner
questions.stem:
A square of side 8 cm and a square of side 6 cm overlap with their sides parallel, as shown. The overlap (shaded dark) is a rectangle 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall.

![An 8 cm square and a 6 cm square overlapping at a corner; the overlap is a 2 cm by 3 cm rectangle, shaded darker.](asset:q32-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the area covered by the two squares together.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the combined shape.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The pieces of the two outlines that are hidden inside the other square are exactly the four sides of the overlap rectangle.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. (a) 64 + 36 counts the overlap twice: area = 100 − 6 = 94 cm².
2. The two outlines together are 4 × 8 + 4 × 6 = 32 + 24 = 56 cm.
3. Inside the small square lie 3 cm of the big square’s right side and 2 cm of its bottom side. Inside the big square lie 2 cm of the small square’s top side and 3 cm of its left side.
4. Hidden altogether: 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10 cm — the perimeter of the 2 × 3 overlap.
5. (b) Perimeter = 56 − 10 = 46 cm.

**Calculation**

- area = 64 + 36 − 2 × 3 = 94 cm²
- outlines = 32 + 24 = 56 cm
- hidden = 2 × (2 + 3) = 10 cm
- perimeter = 56 − 10 = 46 cm

**Why the method works**

A point of an outline stays on the boundary only if it is not inside the other square. For a corner overlap, the hidden parts are the overlap’s own edges.

**Common trap**

Subtracting only 2 + 3 = 5 cm (giving 51 cm), or subtracting the overlap’s area from the perimeter.

questions.title: A staircase cut
questions.stem:
A 9 cm by 4 cm rectangle is cut along a staircase line (dashed) into two pieces, A and B. Piece B is then slid, without turning, to fit against A, and together they make a square, as shown on the right.

![Left: a 9 cm by 4 cm rectangle cut along a staircase into pieces A and B. Right: the two pieces rearranged into a square.](asset:q33-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: What is the side of the square?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: By how much does the perimeter change from the rectangle to the square?
parts.answer: it decreases by 2 cm (26 cm → 24 cm)

parts.label: c
parts.stem: All the steps of the staircase are the same size. How wide and how high is each step?
parts.answer: each step is 3 cm wide and 2 cm high

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Sliding pieces never changes the total area, but it can change the perimeter. The slide itself is “one step across and one step up”.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. (a) Area of rectangle = 9 × 4 = 36 cm². The square has the same area, so its side is 6 cm (6 × 6 = 36).
2. (b) Rectangle perimeter = 2 × (9 + 4) = 26 cm; square perimeter = 4 × 6 = 24 cm. It decreases by 2 cm.
3. (c) The shape becomes 3 cm narrower (9 → 6): piece B moved 3 cm sideways so that the steps fit one place along. So each step is 3 cm wide.
4. The shape becomes 2 cm taller (4 → 6): piece B moved one step-height vertically, so each step is 2 cm high.
5. Check: the staircase drops 4 cm in two steps (2 + 2), and the 9 cm length is split as 3 cm + 3 cm step + 3 cm ✓.

**Calculation**

- area: 9 × 4 = 36 = 6 × 6
- perimeter: 26 cm → 24 cm, change −2 cm
- step width = 9 − 6 = 3 cm
- step height = 6 − 4 = 2 cm

**Why the method works**

Area is the amount of surface, which sliding cannot change. Perimeter depends on how the pieces are arranged: the square is the most “compact” rectangle, so it has the shortest boundary.

**Common trap**

Assuming the perimeter must stay the same because “it is made of the same pieces”.

questions.title: Rooms and walls
questions.stem:
The plan shows a building 15 m long and 10 m wide, divided into five rectangular rooms by straight inside walls (treat walls as lines with no thickness). One wall runs the full length of the building, 6 m from the top edge. Above it, two walls divide the top part into three rooms; below it, one wall divides the bottom part into two rooms. The positions of these shorter walls are not given.

![Floor plan of a 15 m by 10 m building with a long wall across it 6 m from the top; two short walls split the top part into three rooms and one short wall splits the bottom part into two rooms.](asset:q34-fig1)

*The short walls may be anywhere along the long wall.*

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the total length of all the walls, outside and inside.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the sum of the perimeters of the five rooms.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Only the *lengths* of the short walls matter, not where they are: each runs straight from the long wall to the outside wall. In (b), every inside wall belongs to two rooms.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Outside walls = perimeter = 2 × (15 + 10) = 50 m.
2. The long inside wall is 15 m.
3. Each wall in the top part runs from the top edge down to the long wall: 6 m each, so 12 m.
4. The wall in the bottom part runs from the long wall to the bottom edge: 10 − 6 = 4 m.
5. (a) Total = 50 + 15 + 12 + 4 = 81 m.
6. (b) Each outside wall is part of one room’s perimeter; each inside wall is part of two. Sum = 50 + 2 × (15 + 12 + 4) = 50 + 62 = 112 m.

**Calculation**

- inside walls = 15 + 6 + 6 + 4 = 31 m
- (a) 50 + 31 = 81 m
- (b) 50 + 2 × 31 = 112 m

**Why the method works**

A room’s perimeter is made of the walls around it. Adding all rooms counts a wall once for every room it touches: outside walls touch one room, inside walls touch two.

**Common trap**

Trying to find where the short walls are (it cannot be done and is not needed), or counting the inside walls only once in (b).

questions.title: A mirror in an uneven frame
questions.stem:
A rectangular mirror 20 cm wide sits in a rectangular frame. The left and right borders of the frame are each 2 cm wide. The top and bottom borders are equal to each other, but their width is not given.

The outside edge of the frame has a perimeter of 88 cm, and the frame itself (not counting the mirror) has an area of 200 cm².

![A rectangular mirror inside a frame. The mirror is 20 cm wide and the side borders are 2 cm wide; the top and bottom borders are equal.](asset:q35-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the height of the mirror.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the width of the top border.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Work from the outside in: the side borders fix the outer width, the perimeter then fixes the outer height, and the frame’s area tells you how much of that is mirror.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Outer width = 2 + 20 + 2 = 24 cm.
2. Perimeter 88 cm, so outer width + outer height = 44 cm, and the outer height = 44 − 24 = 20 cm.
3. Outer area = 24 × 20 = 480 cm². Mirror area = 480 − 200 = 280 cm².
4. (a) Mirror height = 280 ÷ 20 = 14 cm.
5. (b) The two equal borders share 20 − 14 = 6 cm, so the top border is 3 cm.

**Calculation**

- outer: 24 cm wide, 44 − 24 = 20 cm tall
- mirror area = 480 − 200 = 280 cm²
- height = 280 ÷ 20 = 14 cm
- top border = (20 − 14) ÷ 2 = 3 cm

**Why the method works**

Each clue fixes one unknown in turn. The frame’s area is “outer rectangle minus mirror”, which links the unknown mirror height to known numbers.

**Common trap**

Using 20 cm (the mirror’s width) as the outer width, or forgetting to halve the 6 cm between the top and bottom borders.

questions.title: A chain of overlapping squares
questions.stem:
Five squares, each of side 4 cm, are laid in a diagonal chain with their sides parallel. Each square overlaps the next one in a 1 cm by 1 cm square at their corners (shaded dark), and squares that are not next to each other do not touch.

![Five 4 cm squares in a diagonal chain, each overlapping the next in a small 1 cm square at the corners, which is shaded darker.](asset:q36-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the area covered by the chain.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the chain.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

At every overlap, each square loses 1 + 1 cm of its outline inside the other square: 4 cm disappear per overlap — the overlap’s own perimeter.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. There are 4 overlaps (between squares 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, 4–5).
2. (a) 5 × 16 = 80 cm² counts each 1 cm² overlap twice: area = 80 − 4 × 1 = 76 cm².
3. The five outlines total 5 × 16 = 80 cm.
4. At each overlap, the corner of one square pokes 1 cm along two of its sides into the other square, and the same happens the other way round: 2 + 2 = 4 cm of outline is hidden.
5. (b) Perimeter = 80 − 4 × 4 = 64 cm.

**Calculation**

- area = 5 × 16 − 4 × 1 = 76 cm²
- perimeter = 5 × 16 − 4 × (1 + 1 + 1 + 1) = 64 cm

**Why the method works**

An edge is on the outside only if it is not covered by another square. Corner overlaps hide exactly the edges of the small overlap square.

**Common trap**

Subtracting just 1 cm per overlap (giving 76 cm) or confusing the area of an overlap (1 cm²) with its perimeter (4 cm).

questions.title: A snake of rectangles
questions.stem:
Identical 3 cm by 1 cm rectangles are joined in a zig-zag “snake”: lying, standing, lying, standing, and so on. Each new rectangle touches only the one before it, along a 1 cm piece of edge, exactly as in the picture of the first five rectangles.

![A zig-zag snake of five identical 3 cm by 1 cm rectangles, alternately lying and standing, each touching the previous one along a 1 cm piece of edge.](asset:q37-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the snake made of 5 rectangles.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: A longer snake built in the same way has a perimeter of 92 cm. How many rectangles does it have?

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Each new rectangle brings 8 cm of edge, but where it joins the snake a 1 cm piece disappears from *both* rectangles: each new rectangle adds 8 − 2 = 6 cm.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. One rectangle alone has perimeter 2 × (3 + 1) = 8 cm.
2. Adding a rectangle adds its 8 cm, but the 1 cm join is hidden on the new rectangle and on the old one: +8 − 2 = +6 cm.
3. (a) 5 rectangles: 8 + 4 × 6 = 32 cm.
4. (b) 92 − 8 = 84 cm comes from added rectangles, and 84 ÷ 6 = 14. So there are 1 + 14 = 15 rectangles.

**Calculation**

- first rectangle: 8 cm
- each extra rectangle: +6 cm
- (a) 8 + 4 × 6 = 32 cm
- (b) (92 − 8) ÷ 6 = 14  →  15 rectangles

**Why the method works**

Following one rule (“each join hides 1 cm on two rectangles”) gives a simple growing pattern, which can then be run backwards from 92 cm.

**Common trap**

Thinking each join hides only 1 cm in total (adding 7 cm per rectangle), or using 8 × the number of rectangles.

questions.title: Two notches from two clues
questions.stem:
Two identical rectangular notches are cut from a 12 cm by 9 cm rectangle: one from the middle of the top edge and one from the middle of the bottom edge, neither touching a corner.

The shape that remains has an area of 84 cm² and a perimeter of 54 cm. Find the width and the depth of each notch.

![A 12 cm by 9 cm rectangle with two identical rectangular notches, one cut from the middle of the top edge and one from the middle of the bottom edge.](asset:q38-fig1)
questions.answer: Each notch is 4 cm wide and 3 cm deep.

solution.answer: Each notch is 4 cm wide and 3 cm deep.
solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The perimeter clue involves only the *depth* (each middle notch adds twice its depth), while the area clue involves width × depth. Use the perimeter first.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Area removed = 12 × 9 − 84 = 108 − 84 = 24 cm², so each notch has area 12 cm².
2. Perimeter of the full rectangle = 2 × (12 + 9) = 42 cm.
3. Each notch in the middle of an edge adds twice its depth. Two notches add four depths: 42 + 4 × depth = 54, so 4 × depth = 12 and depth = 3 cm.
4. Width = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm.
5. Check: the notches fit (3 + 3 = 6 is less than 9, and 4 is less than 12) ✓.

**Calculation**

- removed area = 108 − 84 = 24 cm²  →  12 cm² each
- 42 + 4 × depth = 54  →  depth = 3 cm
- width = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 cm

**Why the method works**

A middle notch replaces its own width along the edge with an equal bottom edge, so its width never affects the perimeter; only its two sides are new. That separates the two unknowns.

**Common trap**

Trying to use the notch width in the perimeter, or forgetting there are two notches (getting a depth of 6 cm, which would not even fit).

questions.title: Which perimeters can be found?
questions.stem:
All corners of shapes P and Q are right angles. Only the marked lengths are known.

![Shape P: a staircase shape whose steps go down from left to right; only the bottom (10 cm) and the left side (8 cm) are marked.](asset:q39-fig1)

![Shape Q: a rectangle with a notch cut from the middle of its top edge; marked are the bottom (10 cm), the left side (8 cm) and the notch width (3 cm). The notch depth is not marked.](asset:q39-fig2)

*Shape Q is drawn with one possible notch depth.*

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of shape P, or explain why it cannot be found.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of shape Q, or explain why it cannot be found. If it cannot, say what single extra measurement would be enough.
parts.answer: It cannot be found: it equals 36 cm + 2 × (depth of the notch), and the depth is not given — for example, depth 2 cm gives 40 cm but depth 5 cm gives 46 cm. The depth of the notch would be enough.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

The “push the edges out to the surrounding rectangle” shortcut works only when the boundary never doubles back. A notch makes the boundary go down into the shape and back up again by an amount the drawing does not tell you.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. P: the edges facing upwards (the top and the step tops) together span the full width, 10 cm, just like the bottom. The edges going down on the right (the step sides and the right end) add up to the full height, 8 cm, just like the left side.
2. (a) Perimeter of P = 10 + 10 + 8 + 8 = 36 cm.
3. Q: horizontally, the top pieces plus the bottom of the notch again make 10 cm, and the bottom is 10 cm. Vertically, there are the two 8 cm sides *and* the two sides of the notch.
4. So perimeter of Q = 36 cm + 2 × (depth). With depth 2 cm it is 40 cm; with depth 5 cm it is 46 cm. Both shapes fit every marked length.
5. (b) The perimeter of Q cannot be found. Knowing the depth of the notch would settle it.

**Calculation**

- P: 2 × (10 + 8) = 36 cm
- Q: 36 + 2 × depth
- depth 2 → 40 cm;  depth 5 → 46 cm

**Why the method works**

A perimeter can be found exactly when every edge can be matched with known lengths. In P every edge slides out to the bounding rectangle; in Q, the two notch sides have no partners.

**Common trap**

Using the bounding-rectangle shortcut on Q and answering 36 cm, or measuring the drawing to guess the depth.

questions.title: A sliding copy
questions.stem:
Two identical 10 cm by 6 cm rectangles overlap. The second is a copy of the first slid some whole number of centimetres to the right and some whole number of centimetres down, without turning. The overlap (shaded dark) is a rectangle with perimeter 14 cm and area 12 cm².

![Two identical 10 cm by 6 cm rectangles, the second slid right and down so that they overlap in a smaller rectangle at the corner.](asset:q40-fig1)

*One possible slide is drawn.*

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the combined shape.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find its area.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: Can you tell exactly how far the copy was slid to the right? Explain.
parts.answer: No. The overlap could be 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall (slid 6 cm right and 3 cm down) or 3 cm wide and 4 cm tall (slid 7 cm right and 2 cm down). Both fit all the facts.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

For a corner overlap, the combined outline loses exactly the overlap’s perimeter, whatever its shape. So (a) and (b) need only the overlap’s perimeter and area, not its sides.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. (a) The two outlines total 2 × 32 = 64 cm. The parts of each outline lying inside the other rectangle are exactly the four sides of the overlap: 14 cm. Perimeter = 64 − 14 = 50 cm.
2. (b) Area = 60 + 60 − 12 = 108 cm².
3. (c) The overlap’s width + height = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm, and width × height = 12 cm². So the sides are 3 cm and 4 cm — but which is the width?
4. If the overlap is 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall, the copy moved 10 − 4 = 6 cm right and 6 − 3 = 3 cm down. If it is 3 cm wide and 4 cm tall, the copy moved 7 cm right and 2 cm down.
5. Both slides are possible, so the slide cannot be told exactly. (The drawing shows the first case, but drawings are not evidence.)

**Calculation**

- (a) 64 − 14 = 50 cm
- (b) 120 − 12 = 108 cm²
- overlap: sides add to 7, multiply to 12  →  3 and 4
- slides: 6 right & 3 down, or 7 right & 2 down

**Why the method works**

The combined shape’s boundary is “both outlines minus the parts that are covered”, and for a corner overlap the covered parts form the overlap’s rectangle. Swapping width and height keeps every given number the same, which is why (c) has two answers.

**Common trap**

Reading the overlap’s orientation from the picture and answering “6 cm” in (c) as if it were certain.

questions.title: Two diamonds in a box
questions.stem:
Two identical squares are placed inside a rectangle. Each square *stands on a corner*: one diagonal is horizontal and the other is vertical.

- The squares touch at exactly one point: the right corner of the first square is the left corner of the second.
- The top and bottom corners of both squares lie on the top and bottom sides of the rectangle.
- The left corner of the first square lies on the left side of the rectangle, and the right corner of the second square lies on the right side.

Each diagonal of each square is 6 cm long. Find the perimeter of the rectangle.

![A rectangle containing two identical squares standing on their corners, side by side, touching each other at one point. Each square touches the top and bottom of the rectangle; the outer corners touch the left and right sides. One diagonal is marked 6 cm. Contact points are marked with dots.](asset:q41-fig1)

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

For a square standing on a corner, its total width (left corner to right corner) is its horizontal diagonal, and its total height is its vertical diagonal. The side of the square is never needed.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. The rectangle’s height runs from its top side to its bottom side. A square’s top and bottom corners lie on those sides, so the height equals a vertical diagonal: 6 cm.
2. The left and right corners of each square are halfway down, so both horizontal diagonals lie on the same middle line of the rectangle.
3. Along that line, from the left side to the right side: the first horizontal diagonal (6 cm), then — starting at the touching point — the second (6 cm). Width = 12 cm.
4. Perimeter = 2 × (12 + 6) = 36 cm.

**Calculation**

- height = vertical diagonal = 6 cm
- width = 6 + 6 = 12 cm
- perimeter = 2 × (12 + 6) = 36 cm

**Why the method works**

A diagonal joins opposite corners. When a square stands on a corner, its leftmost and rightmost points are the ends of the horizontal diagonal, so that diagonal *is* its width; the vertical diagonal is its height.

**Common trap**

Treating 6 cm as the side of each square, or trying to add up the slanted sides. The slanted sides are not horizontal, so they do not measure the width.

topics: Geometry > Rotated squares and diagonal reasoning

questions.title: Three diamonds, half the box
questions.stem:
Three identical squares stand on their corners in a row inside a rectangle. Neighbouring squares touch corner to corner, every square touches the top and bottom sides of the rectangle with its top and bottom corners, and the two end squares touch the left and right sides. Each diagonal of each square is 8 cm.

![A rectangle containing three identical squares standing on their corners in a row, touching corner to corner and touching all four sides of the rectangle. One vertical diagonal is marked 8 cm.](asset:q42-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Find the perimeter of the rectangle.

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the area of one square.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: Find the area of the part of the rectangle not covered by the squares.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Each square sits in its own 8 cm by 8 cm box, touching the middle of each side of the box. Its two diagonals split the box into four 4 cm by 4 cm squares, and each side of the tilted square cuts one of these exactly in half. So the tilted square is *half* of its box.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. (a) Height = a vertical diagonal = 8 cm; width = three horizontal diagonals = 24 cm. Perimeter = 2 × (24 + 8) = 64 cm.
2. Split the rectangle into three 8 × 8 boxes, one around each square.
3. In one box, the square’s diagonals are the lines joining the midpoints of the box’s opposite sides. They cut the box into four small 4 × 4 squares.
4. Each side of the tilted square is a diagonal of one small square, cutting it into two equal triangles: one inside the tilted square, one outside.
5. (b) So the tilted square is half of its box: 8 × 8 ÷ 2 = 32 cm².
6. (c) Uncovered area = 24 × 8 − 3 × 32 = 192 − 96 = 96 cm² — exactly half the rectangle.

**Calculation**

- (a) 2 × (24 + 8) = 64 cm
- (b) 8 × 8 ÷ 2 = 32 cm²
- (c) 192 − 96 = 96 cm²

**Why the method works**

Folding the four corner triangles of a box inwards covers the tilted square exactly. That is why the area of a square is “diagonal × diagonal ÷ 2”.

**Common trap**

Using 8 × 8 = 64 cm² as the area of a square whose *diagonal* (not side) is 8 cm.

topics: Geometry > Rotated squares and diagonal reasoning

questions.title: Stacked diamonds
questions.stem:
Two identical squares stand on their corners, one above the other: the bottom corner of the upper square is the top corner of the lower square. They fit inside an upright rectangle so that the upper square’s top corner lies on the top side, the lower square’s bottom corner lies on the bottom side, and the left and right corners of both squares lie on the left and right sides.

The perimeter of the rectangle is 54 cm.

![A tall rectangle containing two identical squares standing on their corners, stacked one above the other and touching at one point; all outer corners touch the sides of the rectangle.](asset:q43-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long is each diagonal of the squares?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: What is the area of one square?

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Write the rectangle in diagonals: it is 1 diagonal wide and 2 diagonals tall, so its perimeter is 6 diagonals.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Width of the rectangle = one horizontal diagonal (left corner to right corner of a square).
2. Height = two vertical diagonals (the squares are stacked corner to corner).
3. Perimeter = 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 6 diagonals = 54 cm, so (a) one diagonal = 9 cm.
4. (b) A square standing on a corner is half of its 9 cm by 9 cm box: 9 × 9 ÷ 2 = 81 ÷ 2 = 40½ cm².

**Calculation**

- perimeter = 6 diagonals = 54 cm  →  diagonal = 9 cm
- area = 9 × 9 ÷ 2 = 40½ cm²

**Why the method works**

Measuring everything in “diagonals” turns the picture into simple counting, just like measuring in tile sides.

**Common trap**

Dividing 54 by 4 as if the rectangle were a square, or using 9 × 9 = 81 cm² as the area of a square whose diagonal is 9 cm.

topics: Geometry > Rotated squares and diagonal reasoning

questions.title: The midpoint square
questions.stem:
The midpoints of the sides of a square tile 12 cm by 12 cm are joined to make a tilted square, as shown.

![A 12 cm square tile with the midpoints of its sides joined to form a tilted square inside it. Tick marks show each side of the tile cut into two equal halves.](asset:q44-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: How long is each diagonal of the tilted square?

parts.label: b
parts.stem: Find the area of the tilted square.

parts.label: c
parts.stem: Without measuring, decide whether the side of the tilted square is more or less than 8 cm. Explain.
parts.answer: More than 8 cm (it is between 8 cm and 9 cm), because side × side = 72 and 8 × 8 = 64 is too small while 9 × 9 = 81 is too big.

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Each diagonal of the tilted square joins the midpoints of two opposite sides of the tile, so it is exactly as long as the tile. The area then follows from “half the box”.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. (a) One diagonal joins the midpoints of the top and bottom sides: it runs straight down the tile, 12 cm. The other joins the midpoints of the left and right sides: also 12 cm.
2. (b) The diagonals cut the tile into four 6 × 6 squares, and each side of the tilted square cuts one of these in half. Area = 12 × 12 ÷ 2 = 72 cm².
3. (c) The area of any square is side × side. Here side × side = 72.
4. A side of 8 cm would give only 64 cm², and 9 cm would give 81 cm². So the side lies between 8 cm and 9 cm: more than 8 cm.

**Calculation**

- diagonals = 12 cm
- area = 12 × 12 ÷ 2 = 72 cm²
- 8 × 8 = 64 \< 72 \< 81 = 9 × 9

**Why the method works**

For a square standing on a corner, the diagonal is the easy length to use; the side can be squeezed between whole numbers using the area, without any advanced method.

**Common trap**

Thinking the side of the tilted square is 6 cm (half the tile) — that is the distance from a corner of the tile to a midpoint, not the tilted side.

topics: Geometry > Rotated squares and diagonal reasoning

questions.title: Side or diagonal?
questions.stem:
Square P has sides of 6 cm and sits upright. Square Q has *diagonals* of 6 cm and stands on a corner. Q is drawn inside the dashed upright box that just holds it.

![Left: upright square P with side 6 cm. Right: square Q standing on a corner, whose horizontal diagonal is 6 cm, inside a dashed upright box.](asset:q45-fig1)

parts.label: a
parts.stem: Which square has the larger area, and how many times larger is it?
parts.answer: P (36 cm²) is twice as large as Q (18 cm²).

parts.label: b
parts.stem: What are the width and height of the smallest upright rectangle that holds each square?

solution.explanation:
**Key insight**

Both squares need exactly the same 6 cm by 6 cm box, but P fills the box completely while Q fills only half of it.

**Step-by-step reasoning**

1. Area of P = 6 × 6 = 36 cm².
2. Q stands on a corner with diagonals of 6 cm, so its box is 6 cm by 6 cm, and Q is half of that box: 36 ÷ 2 = 18 cm².
3. (a) P is larger: 36 ÷ 18 = 2 times as large.
4. (b) P’s smallest upright box is P itself: 6 cm by 6 cm. Q’s width and height are its two diagonals: also 6 cm by 6 cm.

**Calculation**

- P: 6 × 6 = 36 cm²
- Q: 6 × 6 ÷ 2 = 18 cm²
- 36 ÷ 18 = 2

**Why the method works**

A diagonal is longer than a side. Q’s diagonal is 6 cm, so Q’s side is shorter than 6 cm, and Q must be the smaller square — exactly half, because it is half of its box.

**Common trap**

Assuming “6 cm” describes the same square in both cases and answering that the areas are equal.

topics: Geometry > Rotated squares and diagonal reasoning

questions.title: Diamonds with gaps
questions.stem:
Four identical squares stand on their corners in a row inside a rectangle. Each square’s diagonals are 7 cm. Between each square and the next there is a gap of 2 cm, measured from the right corner of one square to the left corner of the next, along the middle line. Every square touches the top and bottom sides of the rectangle, and the end squares touch the left and right sides.
